system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-12-05 16:01:00 to 2176-12-11 18:39:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with weakness and confusion due to malignant hypercalcemia in the setting of relapsed refractory multiple myeloma. He had recently received pamidronate, so he was treated with IV fluids and nasal calcitonin instead. His hospital course was complicated by steroid-induced hyperglycemia requiring an insulin drip and subsequent insulin regimen adjustment, with glargine increased to 35 units nightly. His renal function fluctuated but stabilized with careful fluid management. He reported dyspnea on exertion, but imaging and V/Q scan ruled out pulmonary embolism or significant fluid overload; a pharmacologic stress test was arranged outpatient to evaluate for cardiac causes. He remained on oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis and continued chemotherapy with bortezomib and dexamethasone. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor blood glucose four times daily, follow up with endocrinology and oncology, and schedule a cardiac stress test.

BRIEF SUMMARY

Mr. ___ is a ___ with relapsed refractory multiple myeloma s/p 
autologous transplant (___) and several chemotherapy 
regimens, h/o bilateral PEs, HTN, DM II who presented with 
malignant hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, and an acute kidney 
injury after being discharged two days prior for the same issue. 


#Malignant hypercalcemia:
Pt presented to clinic and was found to have a calcium of 11.8. 
Of note, he was discharged only two days prior to admission for 
the same issue. His hypercalcemia is likely secondary to his 
multiple myeloma exacerbated by dehydration in the setting of 
osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia. He was treated with fluids, 
and given bortezomib, dexamethasone 20 mg daily for 4 days, and 
cyclophosphamide with normalization of his calcium. He was 
scheduled to follow up with Dr. ___ primary 
hematologist, the day after discharge.

#Hyperglycemia:
Pt with history of uncontrolled DMII, followed by ___ as an 
outpatient. His hyperglycemia is likely due to his dexamethasone 
therapy as part of his multiple myeloma treatment, in addition 
to inconsistent adherence to his diabetes treatment plan. 
Initially, he required an insulin drip, however after 
consultation with ___ he was able to be transitioned to 
Lantus and a sliding scale. After some adjustment, his sugars 
were reasonably well-controlled. He was instructed to check his 
blood sugars four times daily and to follow up with his 
endocrinologist after discharge.

#HCAP Pneumonia:
During his course, he c/o a new cough, and a CXR revealed a left 
middle lung consolidation c/f pneumonia. He was initially 
started on azithromycin, however experienced a transaminitis so 
was transitioned to Levofloxacin. He remained afebrile with good 
oxygen saturations. He was discharged to complete a total of 8 
days of antibiotics.

___ on CKD: Pt initially noted in clinic  have a creatinine of 
1.9 up from a baseline of 1.1-1.2. Cr elevation likely from 
osmotic diuresis in setting of hyperglycemia, although likely 
contribution from advancing multiple myeloma as well. He was 
treated with aggressive fluid resuscitation with normalization 
of his creatinine.

Transaminitis: 
Patient experienced a transaminitis after receiving 
azithromycin. Abx were switched to levofloxacin with improvement 
in LFTs, although his ALT remained elevated at 47 at discharge.

# Refractory IgA Lambda Multiple Myeloma: Disease appears to be 
advancing despite previous autologous transplant and several 
chemotherapy regimens. While inpatient, patient received cycle 2 
of bortezomib and dexamethasone, this time with cyclophosphamide 
added. He was continued on acyclovir and Bactrim DS for 
prophylaxis and was scheduled to follow up with Dr. ___, 
___ hematologist, the day after discharge. 

# Hx of PE: Not on anticoagulation due to thrombocytopenia; 
underwent V/Q scan on ___ (prior admission) after experiencing 
DOE which showed a low likelihood of PE. Pt maintained good 
oxygen saturations and did not report any chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You were brought in today because of weakness and confusion. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really weak since this morning. I felt confused when I woke up. I’ve been trying to drink more water and eat well since I got home last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood work shows your calcium is high—11.8—which can cause confusion and weakness. This is likely due to your multiple myeloma. We’ll start IV fluids right away to help bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time it was high too. Why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your myeloma is still active, and it causes your bones to release calcium. Plus, your blood sugar has been high, which leads to dehydration and makes the calcium worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My wife said my sugar was over 600 last week. I thought I was doing okay with my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The dexamethasone you take for myeloma can raise your blood sugar a lot. We’ll start you on an insulin drip to get it under control, and then switch to your regular insulin later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my kidneys? Last time they were struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.9, which is higher than your baseline. This is likely from dehydration due to high sugars. We’ll give you fluids and monitor your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my myeloma? Are we changing treatment again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since your disease is progressing, we’re starting a new cycle of bortezomib and dexamethasone, and adding cyclophosphamide this time to try to get better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope this one works. I’ve been through so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing our best to manage it. You’ll continue your other medications like vancomycin for C. diff and lamivudine for hepatitis B.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still tired, but a little more alert. I’ve had a bit of a cough though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray last night because of that. It shows a patchy area in your left lung, which could be pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I don’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not everyone gets a fever, especially with your immune system affected by myeloma. We’re starting you on azithromycin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I need to talk to you about your liver tests. They’ve gone up since starting azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Could it be from my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely the azithromycin. We’re going to stop it and switch to levofloxacin, which is safer for your liver. Your liver numbers should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your calcium is coming down—now 9.8—and your creatinine is improving too, down to 1.5. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve weaned off the insulin drip. You’re back on your glargine at 35 units at night, plus a sliding scale. The endocrine team helped adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep checking my sugars four times a day like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call your endocrinologist if it’s over 250 or under 80. Now, your cough is better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I haven’t needed to cough as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your oxygen levels are stable, and you’ve stayed afebrile. We’ll keep you on levofloxacin for a full 8-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lab results this morning show your calcium is now 9.3, creatinine 1.3, and glucose averaging around 190. All moving in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If things keep improving, probably in a couple of days. We want to make sure your kidney function stabilizes and you’re managing your sugars well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my myeloma? Is this new chemo helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping this combination will slow it down. You’ll follow up with your hematologist the day after discharge to keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show calcium at 9.1, creatinine 1.2, and liver enzymes improving. ALT is still a bit high at 47, but it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting closer to going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home on levofloxacin for two more doses and benzonatate for any lingering cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it as prescribed. Should I restart any of my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your home meds are continuing—vancomycin, acyclovir, allopurinol, and your blood pressure and diabetes meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable. You’re alert, eating well, and your vitals are normal. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep checking your blood sugar four times daily. Take your insulin as prescribed. Finish the levofloxacin, and use benzonatate if you cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have oncology tomorrow, endocrinology next week, and urology for your incontinence. Make sure to attend all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here so soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all working to keep that from happening. Stay hydrated, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. Your wife can bring the car around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in. How are you doing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m doing well. Took the last dose of Levaquin this morning. Sugar’s been between 150 and 200.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep it up, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your hematologist confirmed your appointment is set for today. They’ll review your myeloma status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already on my way. I’ll let you know how it goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got a note from your oncologist. They’re glad to see you’re stable and will continue monitoring your treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’m trying to stay positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Keep following the plan, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll close out your chart now. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s our pleasure. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final lab review shows all values stable. Discharge is officially confirmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to be home. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll be in touch if anything comes up from your follow-up tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—your home health nurse will visit tomorrow to check your vitals and help with any questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have it on my calendar. I appreciate the extra support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to make sure you’re supported. Call us anytime if you’re unsure about anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was readmitted two days after discharge due to recurrent malignant hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, and acute kidney injury in the setting of relapsed refractory multiple myeloma. He was treated with IV fluids, a new cycle of chemotherapy with bortezomib, dexamethasone, and cyclophosphamide, and insulin therapy for steroid-induced hyperglycemia. During his stay, he developed a cough, and a chest X-ray revealed a left mid-zone infiltrate consistent with pneumonia. He was initially started on azithromycin but switched to levofloxacin due to transaminitis. His calcium, renal function, and glucose levels stabilized, and he was discharged home on oral levofloxacin, insulin, and his baseline medications with close follow-up arranged in oncology, endocrinology, and urology.
